question: A programme coordinator is deciding whether a piece of Claude's output should be produced as an artifact rather than as an ordinary reply in the chat. Which two characteristics point towards an artifact? Select two.
options: A) The reply needs to be read once during the discussion and then not referred to again.
B) The coordinator wants Claude to talk through how it reached its earlier suggestion.
C) The content is something the team will edit and reuse well outside this conversation.
D) The answer is a two-sentence clarification of a term used earlier in the discussion.
E) The content makes sense on its own without the surrounding chat to explain it.
correct_answers: C) The content is something the team will edit and reuse well outside this conversation.
E) The content makes sense on its own without the surrounding chat to explain it.
explanations: Something read once and then discarded fails the test of being referred back to, which is one of the reasons for creating an artifact in the first place.
Reasoning about the discussion is conversational by nature. It is tied to the exchange and would not be meaningful as a standalone document.
Correct. Content meant to be edited, iterated on and reused elsewhere is exactly what an artifact is for, since it gives the work a durable home outside the chat.
A brief clarification belongs inline. Putting two sentences into a separate document adds friction without giving anyone something worth returning to.
Correct. Standing alone is a separate criterion from reuse: content that needs the conversation around it to make sense loses meaning once it is lifted out.
